cells.tense: The heading is already set, and the hand on it is steady today.
cells.ask: Name the direction you're already walking, then take one step someone else could see.
cells.core:
You know which way you're heading, and you're not arguing with it. Something that couldn't hold gave way — not a catastrophe, just a clearing — and you're using the open space to pick a heading instead of rebuilding the old shape. The pick isn't loud. It shows in what you stop reaching for.

That steadiness has a carry cost. Holding a direction without gripping it is a live balance, not a one-time win. What this balance is free to feed next is support — strength from other people flowing where it's needed. So let the direction leave your own head. Tell one person the heading and the step that follows it. They don't have to carry you. They just need to see the line you're walking, so the open space keeps pointing somewhere.
cells.sheetLine: Direction set, hand steady, and the pick is already yours.
cells.verb: choosing which direction to head in
cells.place: where something that couldn't hold has just come down

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead the right direction will finally be proven, and one choice after another gets drafted for that day.
cells.ask: Pick one open question and leave it open until tomorrow night.
cells.core:
There's a version ahead where the direction proves out, and you're already there in your head. Options get measured against that verdict before they're lived, so picking turns into more picking, and the open space stops feeling open. You're not lost. You're braced against a future that keeps refusing to arrive.

The steady thing here isn't a better answer. It's being able to leave one unanswered. You can notice what's true without turning it into a heading the same minute. Let one question sit past tonight — not a decision postponed, a question held. What you're hunting for already pulls at you whenever the subject comes up. It doesn't need the verdict to be real.

cells.tense: The pull that used to point somewhere is still there, and the picking stopped a while back.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you've been tending, and where you'd like it to go next.
cells.core:
The pull is still there. What stopped is the pointing. Nothing gets picked right now, so the open space just sits there. You don't need a new light to follow. You need the picking to start moving again.

Don't push on the starved place. It's running low, not lazy. Feed what's still growing. Whatever you've been tending — a craft, a person, a small thing that keeps improving when nobody's watching — say where you'd like it to go, out loud, to someone. Care you've been giving quietly gets named where it can be heard. That's what puts current back through the pointing. Direction comes back through the growing, not through deciding harder.

cells.tense: The steering is already happening and the account of it gets written off to the side.
cells.ask: Write down one direction you're already walking, in your own hand, as something you chose.
cells.core:
You've been moving in a direction for a while — the evidence is in what you've dropped, what you keep returning to, who you call first. But when you talk about it, it sounds like it just happened. Things came up, the path opened, circumstances pointed. Meanwhile the steering has been running the whole time.

The open space after something falls apart doesn't hold itself open. You keep it open by claiming what you've already been picking. Take the simplest form of that: one direction you're walking, written in your own handwriting as your decision. It doesn't need defending or announcing to anyone. It needs to stop being described as something that arrived on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering already. Start putting your name on the turns.

attempts.check: The record doesn't state that the person has been through any actual collapse of a structure, or that they've been defending one — I restrict to how direction behaves in the moment, not what happened. A reader could object that they've followed a clear star for years without any collapse — so the asks stand on their own observation, not on a claimed breakthrough. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you can feel it in the room' — vivid, but it tells them what they're feeling; it's cut. The asks are all things a person could do at home today: one without money, a person, or spare time.
